pick.title: Which of these could you picture?
pick.lede: Here are {n} kinds of work that could suit you. Cross out the ones that feel wrong, until between {min} and {max} are left. Nothing here tests what you can do, so go by what sounds good. You can change your mind at any time.
pick.tooMany: The quiz can compare up to {max}. Cross out {n} more, the ones you’re least curious about.
pick.tooFew: Fewer than {min} feel possible. That’s useful to know too. Send your list anyway, and you’ll get some new ones based on what you crossed out.

quiz.title: Which kind of work would you like?
quiz.lede: {n} quick choices, about {mins} minutes. Nothing here tests what you can do, and there are no right answers. Pick what sounds nicest, even if you think you couldn’t do it yet. Skip any question where nothing fits.
quiz.resultsLede: Sorted by how often you picked each one when it was offered. Read the top ones and notice which description feels right. That feeling counts for more than the number.
quiz.noneAnswered: You skipped every question, so there is nothing to sort yet. You can still open each one below and read what the work is like.
quiz.fewAnswered: You answered {n} of {total} questions, so treat this as a rough hint. Opening the descriptions and reading them will tell you more.
quiz.closeTop: Your top two are close together. That’s common, and many real jobs mix both.
quiz.feelQuestion: Does one of these feel right?
quiz.feelHint: There’s no wrong answer here either.
quiz.feelNoNote: That’s useful to know, not a failure. Copy your results and send them. The next set of kinds of work will be built from what you picked and what you skipped.
quiz.footer: This is a starting point for a conversation, built from {n} questions about what you like. It is not a psychological test, and it says nothing about what you are able to do. Your answers stay in this browser.

signals.title: How to tell a must from a wish
signals.intro: Ads mix fixed requirements with things they’d simply like. A few small words tell you which is which.

wish.label: A wish
wish.words: “is a plus”, “is preferable”, “ideally”, “nice to have”, “an advantage”, “desirable”, “would be great”

must.label: A must
must.words: “mandatory”, “required”, “essential”, or a plain statement with no softening word

neither.label: Hard to measure
neither.words: Lines like “excellent communication skills” describe the person they imagine. Nobody can check them, so don’t count them against yourself.

ads1.ruleText: This is practice at reading job ads, and a way to notice which kinds of work sound good to you. You are judging these jobs. They are not judging you. Job ads are written in insider language, so each one comes with a word list.
ads1.wordsHint: Insider words from the ad, in plain language.
ads1.asksHint: Lines in quotation marks are copied from the ad.
ads1.readOriginalPost: if you’re curious. You don’t have to.
ads1.summaryLede: You’ve now read {n} real job ads from start to finish. Here’s what you said about them.
ads1.nextYes: Open the original ad for a job you liked, and read it with the word list next to you. That’s all.
ads1.nextNone: None of them has to fit. Knowing what you don’t want narrows the search too. The tasks you picked are the useful part: they show what to look for in the next ads.

ads2.ruleTitle: This round works the other way round.
ads2.ruleText: You read the real ad first. Then you choose which words you want explained, guess which requirements are fixed and which are only wishes, and compare your own picture of the job with a plain version. Each job takes about ten minutes, and you can stop after any of them. Nobody is applying to anything today.
